summary: Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834) was a German Reformed theologian, philosopher, and preacher, widely called the father of modern liberal Protestant theology for relocating the ground of religion from doctrine and morality to the immediate self-consciousness he named the feeling of absolute dependence (das schlechthinnige Abhaengigkeitsgefuehl). His On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (1799) and his systematic theology The Christian Faith (1821-22) reshaped Protestant thought and set the terms against which later theologians, above all Karl Barth, defined themselves.
description:
Friedrich Daniel Ernst Schleiermacher was born in 1768 in Breslau (then in Prussian Silesia) into a Reformed clergy family and was educated among the Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuter) before studying at the University of Halle. He became a Reformed preacher, was associated with the early German Romantic circle in Berlin, later taught at Halle, and from 1810 was a founding professor of theology at the new University of Berlin, where he also served as preacher at Trinity Church. Alongside his theology he was a philosopher, an ethicist, a pioneering theorist of interpretation (hermeneutics), and the translator of Plato into German.

Schleiermacher's early and programmatic work On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (Ueber die Religion: Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Veraechtern, 1799) addresses religion's educated critics by arguing that religion is not to be identified with metaphysics or with morality, that is, neither with a system of knowing nor with a code of doing, but has its own distinct province in immediate experience. In John Oman's translation, Schleiermacher writes that religion 'neither seeks like metaphysics to determine and explain the nature of the Universe, nor like morals to advance and perfect the Universe by the power of freedom and the divine will of man,' but is 'neither thinking nor acting, but intuition and feeling'; religion, he says, is 'sense and taste for the Infinite.' This relocation of religion's essence to intuition and feeling (Anschauung und Gefuehl) is the seed of his mature position.

In his major systematic work The Christian Faith (Der christliche Glaube, first edition 1821-22, revised 1830-31) Schleiermacher grounds the whole of dogmatics in what he calls the feeling of absolute dependence (das schlechthinnige Abhaengigkeitsgefuehl), the immediate self-consciousness in which one is aware of being utterly and unconditionally dependent, an awareness he identifies as the point of contact between the self and God and as the common essence of piety underlying the determinate forms of the Christian religion. On this account Christian doctrines are understood as 'accounts of the Christian religious affections set forth in speech,' that is, as expressions and articulations of this pious self-consciousness as it is determined by the redemption accomplished through Jesus of Nazareth, rather than as speculative statements about God in himself derived independently of that consciousness. Schleiermacher is standardly credited by historians of doctrine with inaugurating modern liberal Protestant theology and modern theological method, and his influence runs broadly through nineteenth- and twentieth-century Protestant thought.

In the twentieth century Schleiermacher became the chief representative of the liberal theology against which the dialectical or crisis theology of Karl Barth reacted. Barth, trained in the tradition descended from Schleiermacher, broke sharply with it, charging that a theology grounded in religious experience and human self-consciousness risked making God a projection of the human and displacing the priority of God's self-revelation; Barth's critique is recorded here as his attributed position in that reaction, not adjudicated. Schleiermacher's contributions, his location of religion in the feeling of absolute dependence, his understanding of doctrine as the expression of the religious affections, and his founding role in modern liberal theology, are presented as his own attributed positions.
editorial_notes:
Schleiermacher is described here on Christian and history-of-doctrine terms (neutrality #6). His distinctive theological claims (religion as intuition and feeling; the feeling of absolute dependence as the ground of dogmatics; doctrine as the expression of the religious affections; his paternity of modern liberal Protestant theology) are stated as his attributed positions and not endorsed (neutrality #1, #2). Karl Barth's critique of him is likewise recorded as Barth's attributed reaction, not adjudicated; this mirrors, from Schleiermacher's side, the influenced_by/related edge to Schleiermacher already present in the karl-barth entry, and closes that dangling forward reference. This entry is referenced by karl-barth.

Sourcing triangulates the three Christian lenses per neutrality #8: (a) an academic historian of doctrine and biographer (Martin Redeker, Schleiermacher: Life and Thought); (b) the primary corpus, above all On Religion in John Oman's OPEN public-domain translation, read line by line, together with The Christian Faith; (c) a contemporary scholar on Schleiermacher (Jacqueline Marina, Transformation of the Self in the Thought of Schleiermacher). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

sources.citation: Schleiermacher, Friedrich. On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (Ueber die Religion: Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Veraechtern, 1799). Translated by John Oman. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Truebner, 1893. Primary text, read directly line by line in the open full text. Load-bearing passages verified verbatim from the Second Speech ('The Nature of Religion'): religion 'neither seeks like metaphysics to determine and explain the nature of the Universe, nor like morals to advance and perfect the Universe by the power of freedom and the divine will of man. It is neither thinking nor acting, but intuition and feeling'; and 'Religion therefore is sense and taste for the Infinite.'
